prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with aberration-corrected electron optics (B050) first, and I still regard it as a genuine invention that opened a door: sub-angstrom imaging and spectroscopy of atoms, interfaces and defects is now routine. But the discussion shows that B050 has only my support, and when I test the shortlist against the criteria I apply to the Physics Prize, the optical lattice clock (B013) is the strongest case on the table. It is an invention (Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, 2001-2003, followed by the first strontium lattice clocks) and a measured, verified result (10^-18 fractional uncertainty at JILA, with independent confirmation at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE and NIST and international comparisons). It is an original experiment rather than a later, more elegant one, and it opens a door to things we could not measure before: tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector physics, relativistic geodesy, and the redefinition of the second. All eight of us ranked it, and the credit is the cleanest on the list: two named people, with well-separated contributions (Katori the concept and first demonstrations, Ye the record accuracy, stability and the many-body clock). Maturity is also good, as the technique is two decades old and replicated.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is adjacency to earlier prizes. The 2005 prize (Hall and Hansch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, ion control, including single-ion clocks) sit close by, and the optical comb is a necessary technical foundation for any optical clock. We must be sure that the lattice-clock contribution is distinct and not a better version of work already honoured. The redefinition of the second has also not happened, so some would say the main payoff is still to come. Other groups (Ludlow, Campbell, Bloom, Takamoto and colleagues, and ion-clock groups) built on the same lines, so the two-name attribution deserves a check against the historical record. Finally, I am recalling priority from memory, not from verified documents.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B013 first as a direct step in measurement capability: magic-wavelength trapping removes motional and Stark shifts while keeping the statistical power of many atoms, and many independent labs confirm 10^-18 performance.
responses.response: I agree, and this is the reasoning I use when I judge an instrument-led discovery. The important point is that the confirmation is independent and quantitative, with clock-to-clock comparisons between laboratories, and that is the 'absolutely sure' standard I want. Where I qualify your view is on the comb lineage. Hall and Hansch were honoured in 2005, so our citation should name the lattice clock and the 10^-18 accuracy it reached, and not general optical frequency metrology.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B013 first because the magic-wavelength idea is simple and original, Katori proposed it in 2001-2003 and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clocks, and Ye took the clock to the 10^-18 systematic level and made it a many-body probe.
responses.response: I agree with this attribution and it matches my own reading of who did the original work. I would add a procedural point: because Katori's proposal and first demonstration are separate from Ye's record accuracy, the citation should credit both the invention and its development, so that neither contribution is reduced to the other. I would also ask the committee to examine the early lattice-clock literature, before the 10^-18 era, so that we are sure the priority claim is clean.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B008) first as a clean, original, enabling advance with more than twenty years of confirmation across many laboratories.
responses.response: Circuit QED is a serious candidate and the maturity argument is fair. My concern is attribution inside the credited names. Several colleagues, Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig among them, note that Wallraff, first author of the strong-coupling experiment, is not on our list, and Lindroth also notes the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits. With a name missing from the decisive experiment, I cannot be 'absolutely sure' that the people credited did the original work, so I rank B008 below the lattice clock. I should disclose that you are a Chalmers colleague and that the Chalmers superconducting-circuit programme is close to this field; this does not change my reasoning, but I note it.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators (B048) first, as a new class of matter predicted by Kane and Mele and realised experimentally by Molenkamp's group.
responses.response: I ranked B048 third and I share your view that it is a genuine new quantum state. My difficulty is the same one you raise yourself: the HgTe quantum wells in the 2007 experiment follow the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, and those authors are not credited, with Zhang deceased. The Haldane-Thouless-Kosterlitz prize in 2016 also lowers the novelty margin. I would not block B048, but the experimental part of the credit looks fragile to me and I prefer a candidate where the proposal and demonstration are both clearly attributed.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase (B034) first, as a deep unifying concept confirmed experimentally for decades, and notes the priority questions of Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam and others.
responses.response: I take the importance seriously, and the experimental confirmation (Chambers, Tonomura, optical and NMR Berry phase) is real. But the criteria I use ask for a discovery or invention that can be pinned to the original experiment, and here the priority is spread over earlier theory, Bohm is deceased, and the Berry phase was confirmed by others a few years after the proposal. That is a very different position from B013, where proposal, demonstration and verification can be traced to named people. I would keep B034 on the list but not as our preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, so that it is not second-order recognition.
Whether two names, Katori and Ye, are the right credit, given the contributions of other lattice-clock groups and the many JILA co-workers.
Whether we should wait for the redefinition of the second, or consider the 10^-18 demonstrations and independent comparisons already sufficient.

For my own opening choice B050: attribution between TEM and STEM correctors (Rose, Haider, Krivanek versus Urban, Zach, Dellby), and whether the committee sees it as physics after the cryo-EM Chemistry prize.
statement.conflict_note: I rank B050 (aberration-corrected electron microscopy) first on my own opening ballot, and it is my own field: I am an electron microscopist and President of the International Federation of Societies for Microscopy, so I may know the candidates professionally, and the committee should treat my views on B050 with that in mind and consider recusal for that item. Committee colleague Goran Johansson is also at Chalmers Physics, which may matter for B008 and for general discussion. No specific personal or institutional connection to B013, Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile.
